title: Your First Phone Agent
summary: Half an hour with a voice interviewer that designs your agent and writes the prompt, then an hour wiring it into Vapi until a real phone number answers in a voice you chose. No code, nothing to install.
detail: Two halves. First a voice interviewer asks what your agent should do, who it talks to and what it must refuse, then writes the prompt for you. Then you take that prompt to Vapi, wire up the ears, brain and mouth, and point a real phone number at it. No code, nothing to install.
outcome: A real phone number that answers in a voice you chose, running the prompt you wrote. Not a demo — an actual number on the actual phone network.
prereqs: A Deepgram API key with permission to create temporary tokens.
Headphones and a microphone, on a desktop browser.
A Vapi account to paste the finished prompt into.
artifact: A working phone number the attendee can call, running the prompt written from their own answers.

slides.title: Your First Phone Agent
slides.note: In the next hour we turn the prompt you just wrote into a real phone number a real person can call. No code required.

slides.title: Where we end up
slides.note: You will call a phone number, and something you built will pick up. Not a demo video — an actual number on the actual phone network, answering in a voice you chose.

slides.title: How tonight works — I drive, you follow
bullets: No writing code
No terminal, no command line
No installing anything
Two websites, side by side in your browser
Copy, paste, and dropdown menus
One phone call at the end
slides.note: If you fall behind, put your hand up. Nobody is behind; the whole room is doing this for the first time.

slides.title: Every voice agent is three parts
bullets: Ears — turns what the caller says into text, and decides when they have stopped talking
Brain — reads that text, follows your instructions, writes a reply
Mouth — turns the reply into speech the caller hears
slides.note: That loop runs every time the caller pauses. Round and round, until somebody hangs up.

slides.title: Two companies, two jobs
bullets: Deepgram — the voice. The ears and the mouth: Flux to listen, Aura to speak.
Vapi — the phone system. The number, answering the call, moving audio, hanging up.
slides.note: The brain comes from a third place, Anthropic, and it is in the same dropdown. Three vendors, one screen.

slides.title: Seven steps
bullets: Get a Deepgram API key
Paste that key into Vapi
Create an assistant and set the ears, brain and mouth
Paste in the prompt you wrote during the first half hour
Test it in the browser before you spend a phone number on it
Get a free phone number and point it at your assistant
Call it
slides.note: Everything happens live on the screen. These slides just say where we are and why.

slides.title: That giant thing you just wrote
bullets: What it is: a job description — who the agent is, what it is for, what to say, what never to say
Where it goes: one box, in step 4, called System Prompt
slides.note: Right now: open that prompt in its own browser tab and leave it there.

slides.title: Get your Deepgram API key
bullets: Sign up — no credit card, and you land on $200 of free credit
Give the key any name you will recognise later
Copy it and paste it somewhere safe right now — it is shown once
slides.note: console.deepgram.com → Settings → API Keys → Create a New API Key. Once you close that dialog the key is gone; if you lose it, just make another.

slides.title: What an API key actually is
bullets: Treat it exactly like a password
Never paste it into a chat, a doc or a screenshot
If it leaks, delete it in the console and make a new one
slides.note: It is a password a program uses instead of a person. You are in a room full of people — do not leave your key on screen when someone comes over to help.

slides.title: What tonight costs you
bullets: $200 free Deepgram credit on a new account, no card
$5 free Vapi credit on a new account
Under $0.20 is roughly what tonight’s testing actually consumes
slides.note: The free credit covers a lot more than one evening.

slides.title: Hand the key to Vapi
bullets: Sign up at vapi.ai and open the dashboard
Left sidebar: scroll to Integrations and click it
Find the Deepgram card under Voice Providers
Paste your key into API Key and save. Leave API Url alone.
slides.note: Once it saves, Deepgram jumps to a Connected row at the top. That is how you know it took. Deepgram now bills you directly for speech instead of Vapi passing it through.

slides.title: Create the assistant
bullets: Sidebar → Assistants → Create Assistant → Blank Template
Give it a name you will recognise — “front desk”, not “Assistant”
slides.note: By the end of the night people have four things called Assistant and cannot tell them apart. Vapi fills the three parts with a default preset; we are about to replace all three.

slides.title: A tour before we touch anything
bullets: Cost and latency meters along the top, moving as you change things
Model presets: Balanced, High Intelligence, Ultra Fast, Cost Saver
Three cards: Transcriber, Model, Voice
First Message — what it says when it picks up
System Prompt — where your big prompt goes
Talk to test it, Publish to make it live
slides.note: Note the latency number before we start. Write it down. We are going to make it smaller.

slides.title: Transcriber, Model, Voice
bullets: Card 1 — ears — Transcriber
Card 2 — brain — Model
Card 3 — mouth — Voice
slides.note: Vapi’s names for the same three parts. Each card shows its own latency and cost; the three added together are what the caller feels.

slides.title: The ears: Deepgram Flux
bullets: Transcriber → Deepgram → Flux General English
slides.note: There is a multilingual Flux if your caller might switch languages mid-sentence. The card reports its word error rate — around 2.3%.

slides.title: Flux knows when you have stopped talking
bullets: The old way: count the silence. Too short and it cuts you off; too long and you wait.
Flux: turn detection is built into the model, so it can tell an unfinished thought from a finished one.
200–600ms cut from response time
~30% fewer times the agent talks over the caller
95% of turns detected within 1.5 seconds
slides.note: No timer setting fixes both problems. Understanding the sentence does.

slides.title: And it mishears less than anything else
bullets: 54% accuracy lead on streaming audio — the mode a phone call runs in
47% accuracy lead on pre-recorded transcription
100 key terms you can prime it with
slides.note: Keyterm Prompting is the one to remember: hand it your company name, your menu items, the street you are on, and it stops guessing at them.

slides.title: The brain: Claude Haiku
bullets: Model → Anthropic → Claude Haiku
The edit icon opens a panel with the model dropdown and a temperature slider
Change the model; leave temperature where it is
slides.note: Watch the latency meter. Swapping the default model for Haiku is the single biggest drop you will see all night.

slides.title: On a phone call, fast beats brilliant
bullets: Answering from your prompt is not a hard reasoning task
Cheapest per call, so experimenting costs almost nothing
It is one dropdown — move up to a bigger model later if you need it
slides.note: A caller notices a one-second gap. They do not notice that your agent could have written a better essay. Dead air is what people mean when they say it felt robotic.

slides.title: The mouth: a Deepgram voice
bullets: Voice → search “Deepgram” → Aura or Aura-2 → pick a voice
slides.note: The voice list is long, so search. Aura-2 is the newer one. Preview two or three out loud — this is the part people actually enjoy.

slides.title: The pause before it speaks is what people judge
bullets: 90ms — Aura-2 time to first byte
~300ms — the gap a human expects in natural conversation
3 parts that each add to that gap, every single turn
slides.note: Your caller’s patience is one budget shared across all three boxes. Slow any one and the whole call feels laggy.

slides.title: What it says when it picks up
bullets: First Message → one short sentence
End it in a question, so the caller knows it is their turn
slides.note: Avoid “Hello, you have reached the automated virtual assistant for…” — by word six the caller is already talking over it.

slides.title: Paste your prompt in, then publish
bullets: System Prompt → paste everything → Publish
Length is fine — paste the whole thing
slides.note: Publish is the step everyone forgets. If you change something and nothing seems different, you did not publish.

slides.title: Three things a phone prompt needs
bullets: It knows it is on a phone — no bullet points, no links, no “as you can see below”
It keeps answers short — two or three sentences, then stop
It knows what it does not know — say exactly what to do when asked something outside its job
slides.note: A paragraph that reads fine on screen is forty seconds of someone talking at you. Without the third rule, it invents an answer.

slides.title: Talk to it before you give it a phone number
bullets: Publish → Talk → allow the microphone
slides.note: The Talk button runs the exact same agent through your laptop mic. Much faster to iterate on than dialling every time. It is about to get loud in here.

slides.title: Listen for these four things
bullets: Interrupting — does it cut you off? Check the transcriber is actually on Flux.
Dead air — does it take too long? Check the brain is Haiku, then shorten your prompt.
Waffling — does it go on forever? Add “keep answers to two sentences” near the top.
Inventing — does it make things up? Your prompt does not say what to do when it does not know.
slides.note: Change one thing → Publish → Talk again. That loop is the whole job.

slides.title: Get your free phone number
bullets: Pick Free Vapi number
Enter a three-digit US area code — 415 or 707 if you want it to look local
Press Create. It takes a couple of minutes to go live.
slides.note: Sidebar → Phone numbers → Create phone number.

slides.title: The fine print on free numbers
bullets: One free number per account
US area codes only
Inbound only — it can answer calls, it cannot make them
slides.note: If you see “you have reached the maximum number”, you already have your one free number. The number is free; the calls are about five cents a minute plus what the models use.

slides.title: Point the number at your assistant
bullets: Open your number → Inbound settings → choose your assistant → Save
slides.note: This is the wire between the number and the thing you built, and the one people skip. A number with no assistant attached just rings out.

slides.title: Pick up your phone and call your number
slides.note: Out loud, on speaker, right now. The room should get noisy.

slides.title: Four things that go wrong
bullets: Rings out or a network message — the number is not live yet. Wait a few minutes.
Picks up then silence — no assistant attached. Inbound settings → assistant → Save.
Greeting plays then nothing — it cannot hear you, or the prompt is enormous.
Answers but ignores your prompt — you changed it and never published.
slides.note: Nothing here is broken code. Every one of these is a dropdown or a button.

slides.title: Change one thing, call again
bullets: Swap the voice. Try three and call after each.
Halve the first message. Hear how much snappier the call feels.
Add one rule — “never give a price over the phone” — then try to make it break the rule.
Give it a personality. One line changes the whole call.
slides.note: You now own a loop that takes thirty seconds. Publish after every change, then call.

slides.title: Three knobs, and you can reach all of them
bullets: Ears — which model listens, and how patiently it waits for you to finish
Brain — which model thinks, and the instructions it follows
Mouth — which voice speaks, and how fast it starts
slides.note: Every voice agent you meet from here is these same three boxes with different settings and a longer prompt. You now know where the boxes are.

slides.title: What a real minute costs
bullets: Hosting the call — Vapi — $0.05 / min
Speech to text (Nova-3) — Deepgram — $0.0077 / min
The brain — Anthropic, passed through at cost — fractions of a cent
Text to speech (Aura-2) — Deepgram — $0.030 / 1,000 chars
slides.note: Deepgram is roughly 2× cheaper than the cloud providers on speech to text, and 20–40% under the alternatives on speech.

slides.title: Before you close the laptop
bullets: Save your number — text it to yourself
Save your prompt — keep the version that worked, outside Vapi
Your key still works — it is tied to your Deepgram account, not to tonight
Nothing expires — the agent stays up and answers calls until you delete it
slides.note: It is what you will want to show someone tomorrow.

slides.title: If you want to keep going
bullets: Tools — let the agent look something up or book an appointment mid-call
Logs — every call is recorded and transcribed in the dashboard
Your own number — bring one in from Twilio to unlock outbound calling
slides.note: Reading your own transcripts is the fastest way to improve a prompt. Docs: developers.deepgram.com for the models, docs.vapi.ai for calls.

slides.title: You built a thing that answers the phone
slides.note: An hour ago you had never done this. AI Collaboration Hub · 505 Howard Street · events every week.

flow.title: Your Flux interview
flow.note: About half an hour. Talk it through, then take the prompt it writes with you — you will paste it into Vapi at step 4.

troubleshooting: The interviewer will not start: the key needs permission to create temporary tokens.
It cannot hear you: check the browser microphone permission, and use headphones so it does not hear itself.
Write my prompt is greyed out: talk to the interviewer first — it writes from the conversation.
Your number rings out: it is not live yet, or no assistant is attached in Vapi’s inbound settings.
Vapi answers but ignores your prompt: you changed it and never pressed Publish.
The number rings out or you get a network message: it is not live yet. Wait a few minutes and call again.
